title: Efficient anaerobic sediment processing via a novel sediment core extruder
author: Quinan, Vazco, et al.
materials: protruding from apparatus to a benchtop.

steps.title: Adjust apparatus height and secure
steps.instruction: Remove bolts Item No. 16, 13, 15 from the legs (Item No. 4), lift the top of the frame to the desired height (max core length 2.75 ft), re‑insert and tighten the bolts; place rubber feet (Item No. 9) on the base and, if desired, clamp the corner brackets (Item No. 10, 11) to the benchtop for extra stability.

steps.title: Cap core and insert piston plug
steps.instruction: After core collection, place caps on both ends of the core barrel (Item No. 34). Remove the bottom cap while leaving the top cap in place to create a vacuum. Insert a piston plug—cut from an LDPE rod, lathed to match the inner diameter of the barrel and grooved for O‑rings—into the bottom of the barrel in a single motion as the top cap is removed.

steps.title: Mount core in stopper and lock to frame
steps.instruction: Insert the plugged core into a removable stopper (Item No. 22‑25) that has a matching inner diameter; leave a few centimeters of overlying water to keep surface sediment anaerobic. Ensure the lip at the top of the stopper (≈2 mm wide) holds the core. Pass the core‑tube/stopper assembly through the top plate (Item No. 1) and lock it with the two adjustable brackets (Item No. 12) just below the top plate.

steps.title: Assemble glove‑bag collar and purge with N₂
steps.instruction: Join two plastic gaskets (Item No. 26, 30) with neodymium magnets (Item No. 27) to form a collar that fits around the protruding stopper. Cut a ~5 cm circular hole in the base of the glove bag (Item No. 31). Place one gasket inside the bag and the other outside, magnets facing each other, with the hole centered. Insert the rubber O‑ring (Item No. 28) into the bottom gasket and an additional O‑ring (Item No. 29) around its inner circumference to create an airtight seal around the stopper. Position the assembled collar‑bag around the stopper, then fill the bag with N₂: close all openings, fill, open a small purge flap to vent air, and repeat the fill/purge cycle two more times, sealing permanently on the fourth fill. Place the 50 mL centrifuge tubes that will receive sediment inside the bag and open them slightly before the final purge to eliminate residual O₂.

steps.title: Extrude sediment and collect sections
steps.instruction: Place the bottle jack (Item No. 7) on the baseplate (Item No. 6) directly beneath the core. Raise the jack to push sediment upward until the desired section thickness is exposed. Use a spatula to slice the extruded section and transfer it to a storage container (typically a 50 mL centrifuge tube). The core stopper provides a platform for “soupy” sediment to accumulate rather than flow down the barrel walls.

steps.title: Reset piston and add push rods as needed
steps.instruction: When the jack reaches its maximum height, reset the piston and insert push‑rod assemblies (Item No. 32) beneath it. Each push rod consists of a 6‑inch‑long cylinder (2‑inch diameter) with metal dowels (Item No. 33) and slots for easy assembly. Ensure at least one cylinder has no dowel at either end so its surface contacts the piston or jack flush. Continue the extrusion‑slice cycle, adding additional push‑rod cylinders as needed, until the entire core is sectioned or the target depth is reached.

steps.title: Prepare Fe(II) standards for oxidation test
steps.instruction: Make a 0.1 M solution of Fe(NH₄)₂(SO₄)₂·6H₂O in N₂‑degassed water. Serially dilute to obtain three 20 µM Fe²⁺ standards, each placed in a 15 mL centrifuge tube (10 mL per tube) to simulate pore water. Keep the standards inside the glove bag for the duration of core sectioning (~90 min). After sectioning, withdraw a single aliquot from each tube and analyze Fe²⁺ by the ferrozine colorimetric method to verify that oxidation has not occurred (average recovery reported as 18.6 ± 1.7 µM).

steps.title: Extract and analyze pore‑water iron species
steps.instruction: Section cores at 1 cm depth intervals inside the N₂‑filled glove bag. For each section, extract pore water by centrifugation, then filter the supernatant through a 0.22 µm PES filter inside the glove bag. Measure dissolved Fe(II) (Fe(II)₍d₎) using the ferrozine method. To obtain total dissolved Fe (Fed), add hydroxylamine HCl reductant to an aliquot of the filtered pore water, let the reaction proceed overnight, and then measure Fe(II) again by ferrozine. Calculate dissolved Fe(III) (Fe(III)₍d₎) as Fed minus Fe(II)₍d₎.

description: This novel sediment core extrusion apparatus has multiple benefits compared to similar devices used in sediment research. With many other devices, the core barrel is attached to the extrusion apparatus with a clamp or adjustable collar, which holds the barrel in place while the sediment is extruded. The time it takes to process multiple cores is significantly longer using such a traditional tube compression setup than with the new apparatus described here. With the former technique, even slight compression of the barrel can prevent the extruder piston from traveling the full length of the tube, so the clamped core barrel must be removed and reclamped whenever the extruder piston reaches the clamp. In addition, the core barrel may slip vertically under heavy weight, if relying only on the squeezing of the outside of the tube to hold in place. Instead, in our extruder design, the lip at the top of the core stopper means there is no deformation of the barrel, so the entire core can be sectioned easily, without unclamping and repositioning the core barrel, and the stopper and barrel are easily separated so another core can be slid into place quickly. Extrusion and sampling of sediment cores is often performed at or near the coring location to minimize sediment mixing and reduce the amount of time between core collection and sample preservation and analysis. Because our new sediment extrusion apparatus is a free-standing structure of adjustable height, it can be moved easily to different locations, does not need to be attached to a benchtop or table, can be assembled rapidly, and requires minimal space. This makes it optimal for sampling trips or cruises where space is limited and instruments need to be assembled and disassembled rapidly so other instruments can be set up as needed.
